measurement: Distance from actual rendered content to the bottom of the text area; running furniture excluded.

pageExtensions.text: If the last part of the edge is shorter than one handspan, record that part too. Rounding every result to a whole handspan can hide a difference between the measurements.

Suppose a strip is covered by six equal units, each 2 cm long. Its length is 12 cm. Using units of 1 cm would give a count of twelve for the same strip. The smaller unit gives the larger count. This is why “twelve units” is not enough information: another person must also know the length of one unit. Check this with equal paper strips placed end to end.

A ribbon 3 m long is also 300 cm or 3000 mm long. To check a conversion, ask whether the new unit is smaller or larger. More small units are needed to cover the same ribbon, so the number increases when metres become centimetres. The ribbon itself has not changed. Convert to the same unit before comparing two lengths.

Changing units cannot correct a faulty measurement. An incorrect reading of 12 cm becomes an incorrect 120 mm. Check the original placement and reading before converting. A calculation changes how a result is written; a careful repeat measurement checks how it was obtained.

Before reading a number, trace the length you intend to measure with your finger. Is it the pencil’s full length, including the eraser, or only its wooden part? Two careful readers can report different results if they choose different endpoints. Agree on those endpoints first, then compare the ruler’s position and the readings.
A route distance follows the road, including its bends. It need not equal the straight distance between the two places. State which distance you mean when comparing journeys.

Use the platform clock as a reference for the train. What would you compare in two observations to decide whether the train had moved? A picture of a train does not establish motion by itself. If the train is waiting at the platform, its position relative to the clock can remain unchanged even while passengers move inside it.

Two observations with the same starting and ending position do not prove that an object stayed still in between. A child might run away and return. To check that possibility, watch during the interval as well. When comparing reports, ask not only “Which reference point?” but also “When, and for how long, did you observe?”
This fan offers a different path to investigate. Follow one blade tip, then compare it with the fixed centre. Would one description of motion be enough for both points?

In the playground, choose one seat on the roundabout and one seat on the swing. Sketch each seat’s positions relative to its fixed support at several moments. Both may return to a place they occupied earlier, but do they follow the same path? Use the intermediate positions to support your answer; the starting and ending positions alone may be misleading.

Now design two routes with the same entrance and exit but different total lengths. Add the lengths of all the straight sections between turns and compare the totals. Why is measuring straight from the entrance to the exit not enough? Exchange mazes with a partner and ask them to check your segment measurements before comparing the routes. If your totals differ, locate the first segment on which you disagree. Check that neither person has missed a section or counted one twice.

referenceChecks.glossary: Use the terms together: in “the desk is 120 cm long”, which part is the number and which part names the unit? For a motion description, choose an object and a reference point, then say what changed over time. A path word such as circular adds information, but it does not replace the reference point or the observation.
referenceChecks.summary: Apply these ideas to the bicycle below. On a straight stretch of road, compare the path of the bicycle’s frame relative to the road with the path of a point on a wheel relative to its axle. Why must the reference be named in each description? Then explain what you would measure to check whether successive wheel turns take equal times. A still picture cannot tell you those times: describe the observations you would need.
